datasets.title: Indian city housing listings (asking prices)
datasets.summary: About 5,000 asking-price listings from a fictional property portal in eight Indian cities, posted in 2023 and 2024, plus a small locality table. Prices arrive as text in lakh and crore style, areas come in three definitions and three units, and the same flat is often listed by several brokers. Use it to practise cleaning, honest regression and leakage-safe validation; locality names are real places but every price, distance and listing is synthetic.

dictionary.meaning: Portal listing id (HP-xxxxxx). The exact duplicate rows repeat the same id.
Date the listing was posted, 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-31. Stored as text in three formats (2023-05-12, 12/05/2023, 12 May 2023).
City as typed by the poster. Several spellings per city (Bangalore and Bengaluru, Bombay and Mumbai, extra spaces, lower case).
Neighbourhood as typed by the poster. Case, spaces and a city suffix vary. Joins to localities.csv after cleaning.
Kind of property. Spelling varies (Flat, Apt, House ...). Clean values: Apartment, Builder Floor, Independent House, Villa, Studio.
Bedroom count as free text ('3 BHK', '3BHK', '3', '3.0', '1 RK', 'Studio'). Parse the number.
Number of bathrooms. Some are missing and a few are impossible.
Stated area as a number. Its unit is in area_unit and its definition is in area_type. A few values are impossible (0, 5, 99999).
Unit of area: sqft (square feet), sqyd (square yards) or sqm (square metres).
Which area concept the number means: Carpet Area, Built-up Area or Super built-up Area.
Asking price in INR written as text in many styles ('1.25 Cr', '85 Lac', '85L', 'Rs 1,25,00,000', '12500000'), or 'Price on request' / 'Contact for price'.
Price per square foot printed by the portal, INR per sqft. Blank for some rows and inconsistent with the other columns for some.
Floor of the flat (0 = ground). Blank for houses and villas, and for some flats. A few values are above total_floors.
Number of floors in the building. Blank for houses and villas.
Age of the building in years. Blank when the home is under construction or the poster left it out. A few values are impossible (-2, 150).
Ready to move, or Under construction.
Furnishing level written in several spellings (Unfurnished, Semi-Furnished, Furnished ...). Often blank for builder listings.
Number of parking slots, 0 to 2.
Lift in the building, written as Yes, No, 1 or 0.
Number of listed amenities (gym, pool, club house ...).
Direction the home faces (East, North-East ...).
Whether the project is registered with the state real-estate regulator (RERA): Yes, No or blank.
Who posted the listing: Owner, Broker or Builder.
Synthetic distance to the nearest metro or suburban rail station in km. Blank for some rows.
City name in clean spelling.
Neighbourhood name in clean spelling (real place names, synthetic attributes).
Price tier of the locality: A prime, B good, C middle, D budget or outskirts.
Rough synthetic distance to the city's main business district in km.

gotchas: Price is text in lakh and crore notation with several spellings. Some rows say 'Price on request', and a few prices have the wrong order of magnitude.
Area comes in three definitions (carpet, built-up, super built-up) and three units, so rows are not comparable until you convert them. A few areas are impossible.
The same flat is often posted several times by different brokers with slightly different price and area, and a few rows are exact copies. Random train/test splits leak these twins.
BHK, bathrooms and area move together. Coefficients change size and even sign when you add or drop columns, and the spread of raw rupee prices grows with the price.
Missing values come from different mechanisms: some are structural (floors for houses), and some depend on the hidden value itself (expensive homes hide the price, old buildings hide their age).
The price is an asking price. Who posts it, the listing date and the mix of old and new stock across localities all shift it, so a raw comparison hides the real effects.
tasks: Read both files. Clean the city and locality spellings and join localities.csv. Report how many listings fail to match (it should be only a few).
Write a function that turns price into rupees. Count the 'Price on request' rows and the rows you cannot parse, then print the median price by city in crore.
Convert every area to carpet-area square feet using the ratios in the answer key. Compare price per carpet sqft by city with the portal's own price_per_sqft column.

Find impossible values (tiny or huge areas, floor above total floors, ages below 0 or above 100, 9 bathrooms in a small flat) and prices with the wrong magnitude. Decide for each whether to fix, blank or drop it, and say why.
Find near-duplicate listings (same locality, BHK, floor and an area within a few percent) and remove exact duplicate rows. Build a duplicate group id for later.

Fit OLS of log price on log carpet area and BHK, then add bathrooms, age, city, tier and listing year. Explain why the BHK coefficient changes sign, and compare residual plots for price and log price.
Compare random 5-fold cross-validation with GroupKFold on your duplicate groups for a gradient-boosting model and for OLS. Explain the gap.
Study the missing values in age_years and price. Argue which mechanism (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) fits each, then test one imputation with a missing-indicator against dropping the rows.
datasets.answer_key:
Truth behind the file (synthetic, so these are exact).
Price model: ln(price) = city and tier base + locality effect + 0.86 * ln(carpet area) - 0.05 per BHK at fixed area + type effect (villa +0.18, house +0.06, studio -0.05) - 0.011 per year of age up to 25 years (-0.004 after) + 0.04 for RERA + furnishing (semi +0.03, full +0.075) + 0.035 per parking slot + 0.006 per amenity - 0.022 per km to metro + growth of 5 to 9 percent a year depending on the city (a pooled fit gives about 6 percent) + noise with an sd of 0.10 to 0.18 (larger in prime tiers and in Mumbai). About 3 percent of listings carry a luxury uplift.
Asking premium over the market price: owners about 10 percent, brokers about 7 percent, builders about 2.5 percent. Prices are rounded to attractive numbers.
Area conversions: built-up = 1.12 x carpet, super built-up = 1.35 x carpet (each with some spread), 1 sq yd = 9 sqft, 1 sq m = 10.76 sqft. Your fitted area elasticity should be about 0.8 to 0.9 once bhk and bathrooms are in the model, and about 0.75 if you leave them out. BHK alone looks positive (about +0.37 per BHK) but is about -0.05 at fixed area.
Mess you should find: 4,923 distinct listing ids and 39 exact duplicate rows; about 500 properties posted 2 or 3 times (about 1,200 rows in such groups); 214 hidden prices (MNAR: about 1 percent of the cheapest third versus 10 percent of the dearest third); 25 prices with a wrong order of magnitude; 21 impossible areas; 88 floors above total floors; about 20 impossible ages; age missing for under-construction homes (structural) and for old homes that hide it (about 3 percent for 0 to 5 years, 7 percent for 6 to 15, 37 percent above 15); floors blank for houses and villas (structural).
Confounding: new stock sits in cheaper tiers, so the raw correlation between age and log price per sqft is only about -0.05, but it is about -0.3 within a city and tier.
Benchmarks after cleaning (log price, 5-fold CV): OLS R2 about 0.87 to 0.89, gradient boosting about 0.85 to 0.88. A random split scores about 0.01 to 0.04 R2 higher than a split grouped by property because of the twin listings. Raw rupee prices show a fan-shaped residual plot; log prices do not.

datasets.title: Customer support tickets of a fintech app (Hinglish text)
datasets.summary: About 3,300 support tickets of a fictional UPI, wallet and cards app called PayNest, written in English, Hinglish (Hindi in Roman letters mixed with English), a little Devanagari Hindi and terse chat style, with typos, SMS spellings, emojis and email signatures. It supports category and escalation models, duplicate detection and resolution-time analysis. Several columns are only filled after a ticket is closed, so careless features leak the answer.

dictionary.meaning: Ticket id (T-xxxxxx).
When the ticket was created, stored as text in five formats: ISO with +05:30, dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm (IST), epoch seconds (UTC), 'Mar 5, 2024 2:22 PM' (IST) and ISO with Z (UTC).
Customer id. Some customers write several tickets.
email, chat, whatsapp or phone (phone tickets are call transcripts, mostly in lower case).
Customer plan: Basic, Plus or Premium.
Short subject line. Blank for most chat tickets, and 'Re:' is added on re-sent tickets.
The customer's message. Mixed languages, typos, emojis, signatures and sometimes a quoted reply.
Issue category set by the agent. About 12 percent are wrong, in fixed confusable pairs.
Priority P1 (highest) to P4 set by the agent. It follows customer tier and issue type more than the wording of the message.
Team the ticket was routed to, derived from the agent's category.
1 if the ticket was escalated to level-2 support, else 0. A good prediction target.
Minutes until the first reply.
When the ticket was closed (IST). Blank if still open at the end of June 2025. Only known after closing.
Hours from creation to closing. Blank for open tickets, which is censoring. Only known after closing.
Customer satisfaction 1 to 5. Only about 21 percent of customers answer. Only known after closing.
Y if the ticket was reopened, N if not, blank for open tickets. Only known after closing.
How the ticket was closed (REFUND_INITIATED, ESCALATED_TO_BANK, DUPLICATE_TICKET ...). Only known after closing.
The agent's closing note. Only known after closing.
Id of an earlier ticket this one was merged into. Filled for only some duplicates.

gotchas: Leakage: resolution_code, closing_note, resolved_at, resolution_hours, csat and reopened are filled only after a ticket is closed, so they cannot be features for a model that works at creation time.

Near-duplicates: about 7 percent of tickets are re-sends by the same customer within two days ('Re:', 'Reminder', 'Third time writing'), and about 110 tickets from about 105 different customers describe the same payment outage on 2024-11-22. Only some are marked in merged_into.
The category label is noisy (agents set about 12 percent wrongly, in fixed pairs such as payment failed and refund status), and priority follows customer tier and issue type more than the wording.

Text is code-mixed: English, Hinglish, a little Devanagari, terse chat, typos, SMS spellings, emojis, signatures and quoted replies. There is no language column, and created_at mixes five formats and two time zones.

Concept drift and censoring: the autopay_mandate category exists only from 2025-03-01, 91 tickets are still open (no resolution), and csat is missing for most tickets in a way that depends on how the ticket went.
tasks: Parse created_at into one timezone-aware column (IST). Count how many rows use each of the five formats.
Plot tickets per day and find the outage day. How many tickets arrive between 09:30 and 12:30 IST on 2024-11-22, and what do they say?
Train a TF-IDF plus logistic regression classifier for category on subject and body with 5-fold cross-validation. Look at the confusion matrix and the errors.
Estimate the label noise: read 40 tickets the model gets wrong and say how many look like agent mistakes. Compare with the answer key.
Predict escalated_to_l2 using only columns known at creation time. Then add resolution_code and see what happens. Which columns are leaky and why?
Find near-duplicate tickets (same customer, cosine similarity of TF-IDF above 0.8, within 48 hours). How many are marked in merged_into?
Split by time (train before 2025-03-01, test after) and measure what happens to the autopay_mandate tickets. Suggest what a production system should do.
Compare the csat response rate for slow and fast tickets. Argue why dropping tickets without csat would bias a satisfaction report.
datasets.answer_key:
Truth behind the file (synthetic).
The text is generated from the true category; the category column is wrong for about 12 percent of tickets (pairs: payment failed and refund status, charges dispute and fraud report, login locked and KYC, app bug to login locked, autopay to charges dispute), so about 0.88 is the accuracy ceiling for a text model. A TF-IDF logistic regression reaches about 0.88 in 5-fold cross-validation.
Language mix (generator truth): about 50 percent English, 37 percent Hinglish, 3 percent Devanagari Hindi, 10 percent terse chat. About 5 percent of Hinglish tickets end with a Tamil, Telugu, Bengali or Marathi closing phrase.
Escalation (about 13 percent of tickets) depends on fraud, KYC, charges disputes, amounts over Rs 10,000 and Premium tier. A logistic regression on text, channel, tier and priority gets ROC-AUC of about 0.60; adding resolution_code lifts it to about 0.87, which is leakage.
Near-duplicates: 217 re-sent tickets (same customer, 2 to 48 hours later); about 45 percent of them carry merged_into. The outage cluster has about 110 extra payment_failed tickets between 09:30 and 12:30 IST on 2024-11-22, about 30 percent merged into the first one.
Other facts: 91 tickets are open; about 21 percent of tickets have csat, and the response rate is about 38 percent for tickets slower than 72 hours versus about 20 percent for faster ones; autopay_mandate appears only from 2025-03-01.

datasets.title: Marketplace product reviews (English, Hinglish, emoji)
datasets.summary: About 4,700 reviews of 120 fictional products on an Indian online marketplace, written in English, Hinglish (Hindi in Roman letters mixed with English), some Devanagari Hindi and SMS spellings, with emojis, sarcasm and encoding damage. Star ratings, words and a small human sentiment label do not always agree, and some reviews are fake. It is a good place to practise text cleaning, sentiment models and honest error analysis.

dictionary.meaning: Review id (R-xxxxxx).
Product reviewed, joins to products.csv.
Reviewer id (U-xxxxx).
Date of the review, stored as text in four formats (2024-05-12, 12/05/2024, May 12, 2024, 12-05-24).
Star rating 1 to 5. In some rows it is text such as '5 stars'.
Review title (the first part of the text).
The review. Mixed languages, typos, emojis, HTML entities (&), a few zero-width characters, line breaks and a few mojibake rows.
Whether the buyer bought the product, written as Y/N or True/False.
Helpful votes. In about a quarter of rows it is text such as '3 people found this helpful'.
app or web.
Y if the seller replied. Mostly low-star reviews, replied to after the fact.
Days between delivery and the review.
Human label pos, neu or neg, present for about 30 percent of rows, with annotator mistakes.
Product id.
Fictional brand and product name.
Product category.
List price in INR.
Date the product was listed.
Seller id.

gotchas: Stars and words disagree: about 3 to 4 percent of reviews have mis-clicked stars (such as 'worst, waste of money' with 5 stars), and about 2 percent are sarcastic (positive words, negative meaning).
About 6 percent of reviews are fake: 25 reviewer ids post generic 5-star praise on 8 products in three bursts, none verified.

Text is messy: English, Hinglish, Devanagari, SMS spellings, emojis (some contradict the words), HTML entities, zero-width characters, a few mojibake rows. Many short reviews share the same wording, so identical text alone does not prove copying.
Wrong types and formats: some ratings are text ('5 stars'), helpful_votes is partly text, dates come in four formats, and verified_purchase mixes Y/N with True/False.
Leakage and drift: seller_replied is filled mostly for low-star reviews after the fact, and 6 products lose quality from 2024-06-01, so a time-based split is harder than a random one.
tasks: Load both files and fix the types: parse rating and helpful_votes into numbers, parse review_date, and make verified_purchase boolean. Plot the rating distribution.
Clean the text: unescape HTML entities, strip zero-width characters and fix the mojibake rows (hint: encode as latin-1 and decode as UTF-8). Count how many rows each fix touches.
Build a TF-IDF plus logistic regression model that predicts negative, neutral or positive (stars 1-2, 3, 4-5) from review_text. Report accuracy and a confusion matrix.
Read 40 errors of your model. How many are sarcasm, mis-clicked stars or mixed-language text? Compare with the answer key.
Find the fake-review bursts using reviewer_id, verified_purchase, rating, date and text similarity. How many reviews and products are affected, and how does removing them change the average rating?
Add seller_replied and helpful_votes to the model and see how the scores change. Explain why this is leakage.
Compare a random split with a time-based split (train before 2024-06-01). Check the 6 products whose quality dropped.
datasets.answer_key:
Truth behind the file (synthetic).
Each product has a hidden quality q (sd 0.6). P(negative) = sigmoid(-1.55 - 1.1 * q) before sarcasm is added. In the file about 21 percent of reviews are negative (sarcastic ones included), about 10 percent neutral and about 69 percent positive. Stars given the sentiment: positive 5/4/3 = 68/27/5 percent, neutral 3/2/4 = 55/15/30, negative 1/2/3 = 58/30/12. About 47 percent of ratings are 5 stars.
Planted problems: about 3.6 percent mis-clicked stars (a negative review with 5 stars or a positive one with 1 star); about 2.2 percent of reviews are sarcastic (positive words, negative sentiment, stars 1 to 3); 268 fake reviews from reviewer ids U-15000 to U-15024 on 8 products, all 5 stars, unverified, in three bursts; 68 exact repeated rows and 43 texts pasted across products; about 1.5 percent of rows with non-ASCII text are mojibake; about 2 percent of ratings are text; the human sentiment label covers about 30 percent of rows and is wrong for about 6 percent of them.
Language mix: about 56 percent English, 28 percent Hinglish, 4 percent Devanagari, 12 percent SMS spellings.
Benchmarks: TF-IDF plus logistic regression predicts the three-class sentiment from stars with about 0.85 accuracy and the exact star rating with about 0.62 accuracy (5-fold cross-validation). seller_replied is Y for about 45 percent of 1 and 2 star reviews and about 3 percent of 4 and 5 star reviews.

datasets.title: Streaming film ratings (Indian and international films)
datasets.summary: About 41,000 star ratings from 1,300 users on 950 films in a fictional streaming app, in a MovieLens-like layout of three tables. All film titles are invented, so any match with a real film is a coincidence. The data has the usual recommender traps: a few films get most ratings, many users have almost none, bots and a review bomb are mixed in, and the rating scale changes part-way.

dictionary.meaning: User id. Mostly a number, but about 2 percent of rows write it as text with a u prefix (u0042).
Film id, joins to movies.csv.
Star rating. Whole stars (1 to 5) before 2023-06-01 and half stars (0.5 to 5) after. A few values are impossible (0, 6, -1, 10) or text ('five', '4/5', 'N/A').
When the rating was made, Unix time in UTC. Mostly seconds, but about 6 percent of rows are in milliseconds (13 digits).
Film id.
Invented title with the release year in brackets. Titles come from a small word list, so about half carry a number (2, 3 ...) to tell repeats apart.
One to three genres separated by a pipe, for example Drama|Romance.
Main language of the film.
Release year, 1990 to 2024.
User id. The last three ids are bot accounts.
Age group. Spelling varies ('18 - 24', '25to34') and some are blank.
Gender with inconsistent codes (M, F, Male, female, male, Other, Non-binary) and blanks.
City. Bangalore and Bombay appear as extra spellings.
Date the account was created.
Language the user watches most.

gotchas: Three bot accounts rate about 130 films each with 5.0 inside a few minutes, and one film receives a burst of 0.5 ratings within a single hour (review bombing).
The rating scale changes on 2023-06-01 (whole stars before, half stars after), and timestamps mix seconds and milliseconds, so averages and time-based splits need care.
Ratings contain impossible values and text, user ids with a u prefix, repeated user and film pairs (people who re-rated), and inconsistent gender, age and city spellings.

Popularity bias and cold start: a few films collect most of the ratings, so a 'most popular' recommender looks strong. Many users have 3 or fewer ratings, and 60 films are released late with little history.
People rate what they expect to like, so the observed mean rating is higher than the true average taste over all user and film pairs (missing not at random).
tasks: Load the three files. Convert timestamps to datetimes (check the digit count) and user ids to integers, and report how many rows each fix touches.
Clean ratings: keep only values from 0.5 to 5, drop text values, and keep the latest rating for each user and film pair. Plot the rating distribution before and after 2023-06-01.
Find the bot accounts and the review-bombed film using ratings per user, rating variance and ratings per hour. Decide what to remove.
Plot ratings per film (rank versus count) and ratings per user. What share of users have 3 or fewer ratings, and what share of ratings go to the top 10 percent of films?
Build a leave-last-out split in time (hold out each user's latest rating). Score a 'most popular' recommender with HR@10.
Add an item-item cosine recommender on the same split and compare HR@10 with popularity, overall and for users with 5 to 10 ratings versus 50 or more.
Compare a random hold-out with the time-based split for the same models and explain the difference. Then explain why the observed average rating is higher than the true average taste.
datasets.answer_key:
Truth behind the file (synthetic).
Model: rating = 3.45 + user bias (sd 0.4) + film bias (sd 0.45) + 1.1 * (taste of the user . taste of the film, 5 hidden dimensions) + a language bonus (+0.45 for the user's preferred language, +0.15 for English) + noise (sd 0.65), then rounded to whole stars before 2023-06-01 and half stars after.
Exposure is missing not at random: a user picks films with probability proportional to popularity (Zipf, rank to the power -0.85) times exp(0.9 * taste), so people rate what they expect to like. The mean over all user and film pairs is about 3.4, while the observed mean rating is about 3.9.
Planted problems: bot user ids 1301, 1302 and 1303 (about 130 ratings each, all 5.0, a few minutes apart); a review bomb of about 150 ratings of 0.5 on one film (id in the generator truth) on 2024-12-26 between 19:00 and 20:00 UTC; 2,499 timestamps in milliseconds; 790 user ids with a u prefix; 185 numeric ratings outside 0.5 to 5 and 39 text ratings; about 650 repeated user and film pairs (re-ratings with a later timestamp).
Cold start: about 12 percent of users get only 1 to 3 ratings, about 7 percent are new users in the last month, and 60 films are released between late September and December 2024.
Benchmarks on a leave-last-out split with the bots removed (about 1,070 users with 5 or more ratings): a random recommender has HR@10 of about 0.011, the most-popular recommender about 0.20, and item-item cosine about 0.24 (it helps most for active users).
